utility.notes: Colorado Springs operates its own municipal, four-service utility (electric, gas, water, wastewater) — directly confirmed via CSU's own site. This is NOT Xcel Energy territory, unlike Denver.

value.name: Colorado Springs Utilities (CSU)
value.notes: CSU is a municipal utility; no separate Community Choice Aggregator applies. Net metering: monthly net usage is tracked as 'Energy Sent to Grid' minus 'Energy Provided by Grid'; a positive year-end banked credit balance is paid out on the January bill at the current cogeneration rate, approximately $0.02 per kWh (this is the default behavior for a new solar system or a home purchased with an existing system). Customers may instead opt into a one-time, irrevocable 'rollover' election to carry banked credits forward into the next year instead of being paid out. CSU's own site separately states that in 2026 it 'is exploring options to update how residential solar customers interact with our grid' — an active, unresolved policy review at the time of this research, not yet a finalized change, so no altered terms are recorded here beyond what is currently in effect.

permit_authority.notes: NOT a City of Colorado Springs department. PPRBD is a joint regional authority created by a 1966 Inter-Governmental Agreement between El Paso County and the City of Colorado Springs, directly confirmed on both El Paso County's own site and Colorado Springs Utilities' own solar-process page ('it's the installer's responsibility to obtain the proper permits from PPRBD, which verifies codes and laws. PPRBD inspects and closes permits.'). PPRBD is also the building-permit authority for Fountain, Manitou Springs, Calhan, Green Mountain Falls, Monument, Palmer Lake, and (in neighboring Teller County) Woodland Park — the same permit_authority fact is expected to apply to those jurisdictions too, though each would need its own record with its own utility/county verified before publishing.

permit_url.notes: PPRBD's own domain (pprbd.org) returned a connection failure (ECONNREFUSED) on every attempt this session via both browser and direct fetch — a genuine, persistent block, not a bot-challenge to bypass. This El Paso County page describing PPRBD is cited instead as the best available official confirmation of the authority itself; it is not PPRBD's own solar-specific permitting page, which could not be reached this session.

required_documents.notes: PPRBD's own solar-specific handout (pprbd.org/File/ByAlias/AlternativeEnergyResidential) could not be reached this session (persistent connection failure on the pprbd.org domain).

value: Installer submits a solar interconnection application to Colorado Springs Utilities (CSU) online; CSU reviews it for standards/safety compliance
Once CSU approves, it emails approval and system details to the customer, the installer, and PPRBD
The installer is then responsible for obtaining the proper permits from PPRBD, which verifies codes and laws
PPRBD inspects the installation and closes the permits
After all permits are completed, CSU installs an upgraded net meter and a separate production meter, then issues a Permission to Operate (PTO)
inspection_steps.notes: This is CSU's own description of the combined utility-interconnection-plus-PPRBD-permit process; it does not itemize PPRBD's own inspection steps in detail (that page was unreachable this session).

value.program_or_pathway: CSU Solar Energy Program (Connecting Solar) interconnection application
other_conditions: Residential application fee tier ($100) applies for systems under 150 kW; a separate commercial/large-system tier ($1,000 fee) applies at 150 kW or larger, per CSU's own page
Installer must submit the application on the customer's behalf via CSU's online Connecting Solar portal
System must pass CSU's standards/safety review before approval; if denied, required updates are provided to the customer and installer
PPRBD permits must be obtained and closed before CSU will install the upgraded net meter and issue a Permission to Operate (PTO)

value.name: Colorado Springs Utilities Solar Energy Program application fee (residential)
value.notes: Per CSU's own 2024 rate case, charged on the customer's next electric bill after their solar installer submits the application. This is a utility interconnection application fee, not PPRBD's separate building/electrical permit fee, which was not found this session (PPRBD's own site was unreachable).

value.name: Colorado Springs Utilities Solar Energy Program application fee (150 kW or larger systems)
value.notes: Per CSU's own 2024 rate case; applies to large/commercial-scale systems, not typical residential installations.

value.name: Colorado Residential Solar Property Tax Exemption
value.administrator: Colorado Division of Property Taxation (Dept. of Local Affairs)
value.description: Statewide Colorado property tax exemption: independently owned residential solar electric generation facilities (photovoltaic systems) meeting the criteria in §39-1-102(6.8), C.R.S. are exempt from Colorado property taxation under §39-3-102, C.R.S. To qualify, the facility must be located on residential real property, used to produce electricity primarily for use in the residential improvements, and have a production capacity of no more than 100 kW AC. This is a genuine statewide exemption applicable to any qualifying Colorado residential system, not utility- or city-specific.
value.eligibility: Residential real property, system owned by the residential property owner, electricity used primarily for the residential improvements, production capacity ≤100 kW AC.

rebates.notes: Verified directly from the Colorado Division of Property Taxation's own official page — the same statewide fact already documented in co-denver-denver-xcel.json.
